immunity.recognized_limits: Does not bar criminal prosecution, bar discipline, or injunctive relief. Does not cover investigative or administrative acts. Does not legalize the underlying conduct.
immunity.scope: Damages actions under § 1983 for conduct intimately associated with the judicial phase of the criminal process (initiating a prosecution, presenting the State's case).

immunity.leading_case: Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982); Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223 (2009)
immunity.recognized_limits: Fact-specific; does not apply to injunctive claims in the same way; municipal Monell liability is a separate track.
immunity.scope: Shields officials from damages unless they violated a statutory or constitutional right that was clearly established at the time.

immunity.leading_case: Pierson v. Ray, 386 U.S. 547 (1967); Stump v. Sparkman, 435 U.S. 349 (1978)
immunity.recognized_limits: Acts in the complete absence of all jurisdiction are not immune. Administrative acts may be qualified only. Criminal and disciplinary processes remain available where the law provides.
immunity.scope: Absolute immunity for judicial acts within jurisdiction.

immunity_note: Immunity research is not a recommendation to ignore a shield or to proceed extra-legally.
statute_note: Research catalog. Not charging decisions. Willfulness and agreement are for counsel and a fact-finder.

elements: deprived a person of a right protected by the Constitution or laws of the United States
statutes.research_note: Willfulness is a jury question. A substantiated Brady finding is a factual predicate for counsel, not a completed § 242 offense.
statutes.statutory_maximum: Fine and/or imprisonment up to 1 year; up to 10 years if bodily injury or certain dangerous weapons/threats; any term of years or life if death results (or certain kidnapping/aggravated sexual-abuse predicates).
statutes.title: Deprivation of rights under color of law

elements: to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any person in the free exercise of a right or privilege secured by the Constitution or laws of the United States
statutes.research_note: Requires evidence of agreement. Office custom alone is not a conspiracy.
statutes.statutory_maximum: Fine and/or imprisonment up to 10 years; any term of years or life if death results (or certain predicates).
statutes.title: Conspiracy against rights

elements: took an oath before a competent tribunal, officer, or person
made a statement willfully that the declarant did not believe to be true
statutes.research_note: Requires a specific false statement under oath. Opinion language is not itself perjury.
statutes.statutory_maximum: Fine and/or imprisonment up to 5 years (or up to 8 years when committed in connection with certain offenses).
statutes.title: Perjury generally

elements: the procured testimony was in fact perjury
statutes.research_note: Both procurement and completed perjury must be proven.
statutes.statutory_maximum: Fine and/or imprisonment up to 5 years (or up to 8 years when committed in connection with certain offenses).
statutes.title: Subornation of perjury

elements: knowingly used intimidation, threats, corrupt persuasion, or misleading conduct
with intent to influence, delay, or prevent testimony, or to cause a person to withhold/destroy objects in an official proceeding
statutes.research_note: Subsection selection is fact-specific. Do not charge from a gap report alone.
statutes.statutory_maximum: Varies by subsection; typically up to 20 years. Death-resulting provisions carry any term of years or life.
statutes.title: Tampering with a witness, victim, or an informant

elements: person acted under color of state law
deprived plaintiff of a right secured by the Constitution or federal law
statutes.research_note: Subject to immunity doctrines. Absolute prosecutorial immunity may bar damages for advocacy functions (Imbler v. Pachtman, 424 U.S. 409 (1976)); investigative/administrative acts may be qualified only (Buckley v. Fitzsimmons, 509 U.S. 259 (1993)).
statutes.statutory_maximum: Civil damages, injunction, and attorney fees (42 U.S.C. § 1988). Not a criminal sentence.
statutes.title: Civil action for deprivation of rights
